summary: Instagram is carrying the channel: most Hindi videos get 1,000+ views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly get under 60 views, with only a few older ones reaching 500+. The best videos are about a surprising 'robot or sensor can't see, only senses X' idea, or a familiar gadget with a twist, and they get more likes, saves and shares. Weaker videos are plain 'How does X work?' questions about everyday objects (taps, doors, smoke alarms), which get few views and almost no saves or shares.
winningPattern: Short Hindi videos about a robot or sensor with a surprising 'it doesn't do X, it only does Y' hook (e.g. 'Gyro ke bina robot gir jaata', 'Clap switch taali nahi, shor sunta hai'). Titles are punchy, 6-10 words, in Hinglish with one emoji and #shorts, and name a relatable maker project (robot, clap switch, PIR, mic) rather than a generic building appliance. Instagram is the main engine at 1,200-1,400 views; YouTube works only on a few of these hooks (gyro, clap switch, PIR).
doMore: Use the 'X doesn't do A, it only does B' contrarian hook on robot and maker-project topics
Make follow-ups to the clap switch, gyro, PIR and line follower hits (e.g. a part 2 or a 'what if it fails' version)
Pick Arduino-style builds students can copy over appliance explainers, and end with a question to drive saves and shares
Post the same Hindi video on both platforms and test a stronger YouTube-first title and first-second visual, since YouTube is far behind
Repeat the robot/IR obstacle angle, which got the most shares (10), and ask viewers to share with a friend who builds robots
stopDoing: Generic 'Kaise kaam karta hai? 🤔' titles about taps, lift doors, mall doors, smoke detectors and street lights
Posting several near-duplicate videos on the same sensor (two smoke detector, two IR, two tap videos) in a week
Mixing in English-language videos or leaving a video unposted on Instagram, as the English Arduino Short got no IG reach
